The second charge, the most famous and rhetorically tricky, is that poetry is the "mother of lies." Sidney answers this with a brilliant distinction between affirmation and representation:

Since the poet does not claim that his characters or events are historically real, he cannot be accused of falsehood. A reader who enters a theatre or opens a book of poems understands the rules of the genre; he does not look for literal, historical truth, but for the universal truth of representation.

The third charge is that poetry corrupts the soul by painting lust, promoting effeminacy, and encouraging base passions. Sidney concedes that some poetry is indeed written in a wanton or corrupt manner, but he argues that this is an abuse of the art, not a defect of the art itself. "Shall the abuse of a thing make the right use odious?" he asks. Money can be used for bribery, and the sword can be used for murder, yet no one demands the banishment of money or weapons. The fault lies with the corrupt writers who misuse poetry, not with the art of poetry itself, which is designed to elevate the mind rather than debase it.

The fourth charge is that Plato, the wisest of philosophers, banished poets from his ideal republic. Sidney handles this authority with great care, recognizing that Plato’s name carries immense weight. He argues first that Plato was not banishing poetry itself, but rather the "abuse" of poetry in his contemporary Athens, where poets presented depraved, immoral images of the gods that corrupted young minds. Second, Sidney points out the irony of Plato's position: Plato was himself a highly poetic writer whose dialogues deploy the very techniques of drama, characterisation, and myth-making that he censures. Plato was banishing the false opinions of the deity promoted by bad poets, not the divinely inspired art of the "right poet."

> "To the second, therefore, that because it deals with falsehoods, it must be the mother of lies, of all writers under the sun the poet is the least liar; and though he would, as a poet he can scarcely be a liar. For the poet, he nothing affirmeth, and therefore never lieth. For, as I take it, to lie is to affirm that to be true which is false; so as the other artists, and especially the historian, affirming many things, can, in the cloudy knowledge of mankind, hardly escape from many lies. But the poet never maketh any circles about his imagination, to conjure you to believe for true what he writes. He citeth not authorities of other histories... he reciteth things not as true, but as things which may be or should be."
## A Taxonomy of Genres and the Neoclassical Critique of English Drama

To demonstrate the universal value of poetry, Sidney conducts a brief survey of the various poetic genres, showing how each one contributes to the moral instruction of the community. The pastoral genre, through the humble lives of shepherds, exposes the vanity of courtly ambition and the tyranny of rulers. The elegiac genre moves the reader to a compassionate understanding of human suffering and the transience of earthly things. Comedy, by representing the common errors and follies of daily life in a ridiculous light, teaches the reader to avoid such behaviour in his own conduct. Tragedy, by showing the fall of tyrants and the ruins of ambition, "maketh kings fear to be tyrants, and tyrants manifest their tyrannical humours." Epic or heroic poetry, which Sidney considers the highest genre, presents the mind with images of magnanimous virtue and heroic action, inspiring the reader to emulate the deeds of Aeneas or Cyrus.

Despite this theoretical defence of the genres, Sidney is highly critical of the actual state of contemporary English drama. Writing at a time before the major achievements of Marlowe and Shakespeare, he complains that the plays of the London public theatres are formally chaotic and artistically crude. He advocates for a neoclassical reform of the theatre, urging English playwrights to observe the classical unities of time, place, and action. He ridicules plays that violate these principles by attempting to crowd vast historical narratives into a brief performance:

Sidney objects to these "mongrel tragicomedies" because they violate the principle of decorum, which requires that high and low matters be kept distinct. He complains of plays where "three hours" of stage time must represent the passage of years, or where the action moves from a garden to shipwreck and then to "Asia," showing a character who is born in the first act and married with children in the next. While this neoclassical critique would be bypassed by the spectacular, rule-breaking success of the Elizabethan and Jacobean theatre, Sidney’s insistence on decorum and formal coherence set the agenda for neoclassical debate in England for the next century and a half.

> "For ordinary plays, dear brethren, they be neither right tragedies, nor right comedies, mingling kings and clowns, not because the matter so carrieth it, but thrust in clowns by head and shoulders, to play a part in majestical matters, with neither decency nor discretion... so as the play be neither right tragedy, nor right comedy, but a mongrel tragicomedie."
## The Legacy of the *Defence*

Sir Philip Sidney's *An Apology for Poetry* did not merely respond to a passing Puritan attack; it established the vocabulary and the conceptual framework for English literary criticism. By combining Italian humanist commentary, classical Latin rhetoric, and Aristotelian poetics into a single, elegant synthesis, Sidney gave English writers a sense of the dignity and seriousness of their craft. His arguments would be echoed and modified by Ben Jonson, John Dryden, Percy Bysshe Shelley, and Matthew Arnold, each of whom would return to the central question of how literature can reconcile the demands of aesthetic pleasure with those of moral truth. That the essay remains readable today owes something both to the cogency of its arguments and to the lively, courtly voice of its author, who defended his art by demonstrating in his own prose the very delight and instruction he claimed for poetry.
### Sources and Verification

- Sidney, Philip. *An Apology for Poetry (or The Defence of Poesy)*. Edited by Geoffrey Shepherd, revised by R. W. Maslen, Manchester University Press, 2002.
- Quotations verified against the Oxford World's Classics edition: *The Major Works including Astrophil and Stella and The Defence of Poesy*, edited by Katherine Duncan-Jones, Oxford University Press, 2008.
- The "brazen/golden" passage: Oxford World's Classics, p. 216.
- The "peerless poet" passage: Oxford World's Classics, p. 221.
- The "nothing affirmeth" passage: Oxford World's Classics, p. 235.
- The "mongrel tragicomedie" passage: Oxford World's Classics, p. 244.

chapters.title: 12. John Dryden: Of Dramatick Poesie, An Essay

content.value: John Dryden (1631–1700)
Original title: *Of Dramatick Poesie, An Essay*
1668 · English · England · Neoclassical Period / Restoration · Critical Dialogue
## A Barge on the Thames: The Drama of Criticism Amidst War

John Dryden’s *Of Dramatick Poesie, An Essay* is set against a background of immediate political and physical crisis. The dialogue takes place on 3 June 1665, a day when the English and Dutch navies are engaged in the Battle of Lowestoft during the Second Anglo-Dutch War. As the distant rumble of cannon fire shakes the air of London, four gentlemen escape the plague-ridden city by taking a barge down the River Thames toward Greenwich. The setting is deeply symbolic: the characters are debating the laws of artistic representation while their nation fights for maritime and political supremacy. The naval battle provides a dramatic counterpoint to the intellectual contest on the boat; the struggle for sovereignty on the seas mirrors the struggle for literary sovereignty among European nations. When the naval gunfire subsides, indicating an English victory, the characters turn their attention to the state of English letters, asking whether their country's literary achievements can match its growing political power.

The choice of the dialogue form is itself a major critical statement. By presenting his essay as a conversation among four friends, Dryden avoids the dogmatic, prescriptive tone that had characterized Renaissance criticism, such as that of Castelvetro or Sidney. Instead, the dialogue structure allows him to explore multiple, competing perspectives on dramatic form without immediately committing to a single authority. The conversation operates as a model of Restoration politeness and intellectual liberty: the characters disagree sharply on fundamental questions of art, yet they conduct their debate with mutual respect and rational persuasion. This method reflects the empirical spirit of the early Royal Society, of which Dryden was a member, suggesting that critical truth is not a set of ancient laws to be inherited, but a consensus to be reached through the comparison of evidence and the free play of wit.
## Four Voices, Four Poetics: The Debate Partitioned
The four speakers in the dialogue represent distinct, historically identifiable critical positions, each associated with a prominent figure in Restoration intellectual life.

Crites, representing Dryden’s brother-in-law Sir Robert Howard, is the champion of the Ancients. He argues that the Greeks and Romans established the absolute rules of dramatic poetry, and that modern writers are at best successful imitators who can never hope to surpass their classical models.

Eugenius, representing Charles Sackville, Lord Buckhurst, defends the Moderns. He argues that while the Ancients deserve credit for inventing the dramatic form, the Moderns have improved upon their designs by combining classical structure with a deeper, more refined understanding of human psychology and natural philosophy.

Lisideius, representing Sir Charles Sedley, argues for the superiority of the contemporary French neoclassical theatre over the English tradition. He praises Corneille and Racine for their strict adherence to the Three Unities of action, time, and place, and for their commitment to decorum, which excludes onstage violence and low comedy in favour of elegant, declamatory verse.

Neander, whose name means "new man" and who represents Dryden himself, offers the patriotic defence of the English stage. He champions Shakespeare, Fletcher, and Jonson, arguing that the English tradition, despite its violations of classical rules and its mixing of tragedy and comedy, is ultimately superior because it is livelier and more faithful to the complex reality of human nature.
## The Battle of the Ages: Ancient Rules and Modern Improvements

The opening phase of the debate, carried out between Crites and Eugenius, addresses the relationship between historical authority and artistic progress. Crites bases his defence of the Ancients on the concept of nature. The Greeks and Romans, he argues, lived closer to nature than the moderns, and their rules, such as the unities of time and place, were not arbitrary inventions but direct observations of nature's laws. The Ancients observed that a play becomes implausible if its action covers years or moves across distant countries within the space of three hours in a theatre. Crites complains that modern English writers, in neglecting these rules, produce chaotic spectacles that insult the audience's intelligence. For Crites, the decline of modern drama is the direct result of a failure to copy the classical models: "we draw not after their lines, but those of one another; and this is the reason why we fall so short of them."

Eugenius counters this conservative classicism by arguing for the progress of knowledge and art. Just as the modern era has witnessed major discoveries in science and astronomy, such as the Copernican system and the circulation of the blood, so too has it refined its understanding of the human mind and the mechanics of drama. Eugenius argues that the Ancients were not as perfect as Crites suggests: their plots were often repetitive and predictable, relying on well-worn myths that the audience already knew, and their plays frequently violated their own rules. Furthermore, Eugenius accuses the Ancients of failing to represent the passion of love with any psychological depth, a territory where modern writers have achieved unprecedented sophistication. By pointing to these limitations, Eugenius establishes that the Moderns are not mere copyists but innovators who have built upon classical foundations to create a more complex and expressive art.
## The Channel Divide: French Decorum and the English Stage

The debate then shifts to a comparison between French neoclassicism and the English stage, with Lisideius presenting the case for the French. Lisideius argues that the French stage is the most accomplished in Europe because it respects the rules of decorum and the unities. The French playwrights, he observes, never represent battles or deaths on stage; instead, they employ messengers to report these events in elegant, reasoned verse. This avoidance of onstage action is not a sign of cowardice, but of a superior understanding of theatrical plausibility: a battle represented by a few actors with wooden swords is ridiculous, and a violent death on stage breaks the illusion of reality. Furthermore, Lisideius praises the French for their focus on a single plot, avoiding the English practice of "under-plots" or double plots, which he argues distract the audience and destroy the unity of the dramatic impression.

Neander rejects this French model as cold, bloodless, and lacking in vital energy. While he concedes that French plays are more regular and formally correct, he argues that this regularity is purchased at the cost of dramatic interest:

For Neander, the purpose of drama is both to satisfy the intellect with formal correctness and to represent human life in all its variety and passion. The English preference for double plots and tragicomedy is not a defect, but a natural expression of the English character, which demands a richer, more active theatrical experience. Tragicomedies, which mingle kings and clowns, are truer to the natural world, where grief and joy are constantly juxtaposed. By defending these irregular forms, Neander moves the critical discussion away from the mechanical application of rules and toward a functional assessment of audience pleasure and psychological realism.

> "I will grant Lisideius, without dispute, that the French plays are more regular, and observe the laws of the comedy, and the decorum of the stage, to a beauty; but it is otherwise a very dry; and, as one may say, a masculine beauty; or rather, such a beauty as constantly attends the best-bred women in France, who, if they have not some features which may be called out of design, yet have nothing in them which is not extremely regular. But if our English plays have more plots than one, and that one bigger than the French, it is because we have more variety, and more characters."
## The Twin Giants of English Drama: Shakespeare and Jonson

Neander’s defence of the English stage culminates in his famous comparative analysis of William Shakespeare and Ben Jonson. This passage represents a landmark in English criticism, establishing the terms of Shakespeare's reputation for the next two centuries and defining the tension between natural genius and learned art.

Neander begins by characterizing Shakespeare as the supreme exemplar of natural, uncultivated genius, a writer who did not need the rules of the Ancients because he had direct access to the source of all art:

Shakespeare’s greatness, in Neander's account, is not a product of study or rule-following, but of a unique, intuitive capacity to mirror the human condition. His errors and irregularities are minor blemishes on a genius that surpasses all classical precedents.

Neander then contrasts Shakespeare with Ben Jonson, the writer who represented the peak of English classical learning and adherence to dramatic rule. Jonson, Neander observes, was "the most learned and judicious writer which any theatre ever had." He did not rely on luck or raw inspiration; rather, he constructed his plays laboriously, borrowing from the classical writers and adapting their principles to the English language. Jonson was "a painful observer of mankind," who excelled in representing the "humours" or defining quirks of human behaviour. Yet, despite Jonson's formal perfection, Neander establishes a clear hierarchy of affection between the two writers:

This distinction between admiration (which is paid to Jonson’s art and learning) and love (which is inspired by Shakespeare’s natural genius and comprehensive humanity) became a foundational trope of English literary criticism. It allowed Dryden to respect the neoclassical rules while asserting the superior value of a distinctively English, irregular genius.

> "To begin, then, with Shakespeare. He was the man who of all modern, and perhaps ancient poets, had the largest and most comprehensive soul. All the images of Nature were still present to him, and he drew them, not laboriously, but luckily; when he describes anything, you more than see it, you feel it too. Those who accuse him to have wanted learning, give him the greater commendation: he was naturally learned; he needed not the spectacles of books to read Nature; he looked inward, and found her there."

> "If I would compare him with Shakespeare, I must acknowledge him the more correct writer, but Shakespeare the greater wit. Shakespeare was the Homer, or father of our dramatic poets; Jonson was the Virgil, the pattern of elaborate writing; I admire him, but I love Shakespeare."
## The Debate on Rhyme: Elevating Tragedy above the Common Tongue

The final section of the essay consists of a debate between Crites and Neander on the use of rhymed couplets in tragedy. Crites argues against rhyme, asserting that because drama is an imitation of human speech, it should employ the most natural language possible. Blank verse, he suggests, is closer to the rhythms of ordinary conversation, whereas rhymed couplets sound artificial and constrained, forcing characters to speak in unnatural patterns that break the dramatic illusion. For Crites, rhyme is an ornament that belongs to lyric poetry, not to the stage: "no man without doubt writes in rhyme as he would speak in prose; and therefore, since play is an imitation of human life, it ought to be written in a style that is most natural to it."

Neander defends the use of rhyme in tragedy by redefining the relationship between art and nature. Tragedy, he argues, is not a literal transcription of common life, but an elevated representation of heroic actions and passions. As such, it requires a language that is superior to ordinary speech. Rhyme provides this elevation, helping the poet to control his imagination and giving the verse a dignity and polish that blank verse lacks. Neander suggests that a tragedy written in rhyme is like a painting that uses rich colours to represent a noble subject: it does not seek to deceive the viewer into thinking the object is real, but to make the representation more beautiful and memorable. This defence of rhyme reflects the aesthetic preferences of the early Restoration court, which favoured the heroic play as a means of celebrating royal authority and aristocratic virtue after the disruptions of the Civil War.
## A Restoration Settlement for the English Stage

*Of Dramatick Poesie* ends without a formal verdict. As the barge reaches its destination at Somerset Stairs, the characters step ashore, their debate unresolved but their friendships intact. This open ending is central to Dryden’s critical purpose. By refusing to declare a definitive winner among the competing positions, Dryden invites the reader to participate in an ongoing, dialectical process of evaluation. The essay does not impose a single, dogmatic system of rules; instead, it establishes criticism as a space of free, polite discussion. Through Neander’s arguments, Dryden succeeds in vindicating the English dramatic tradition against French hegemony and classical dogmatism, while still respecting the values of order, decorum, and learning. The essay is a critical settlement for the Restoration stage, clearing a space for a modern English literature that is regular without being cold, and free without being chaotic.
### Sources and Verification

chapters.title: 13. Aphra Behn: Preface to The Lucky Chance

content.value: Aphra Behn (1640–1689)
Original title: Preface to *The Lucky Chance; or, An Alderman's Bargain*
1686 (published with the play) · English · England · Restoration Drama · Preface / Feminist Apologia
## The Hostile Stage: Sexism and Censorship in Restoration London

Aphra Behn’s Preface to *The Lucky Chance* (1686) is a foundational document in the history of feminist literary criticism and professional authorship in England. Written to accompany the publication of her comedy *The Lucky Chance; or, An Alderman's Bargain*, the Preface represents a fierce response to the hostile environment of the late Restoration theatre. Although Behn was one of the most successful and prolific playwrights of the era, her position as a self-supporting female writer made her a target for systematic hostility. The staging of *The Lucky Chance* had been met with accusations of "bawdiness" and indecency, with critics claiming that the play's representation of sexual intrigue and forced marriage was unfit for a polite audience. Behn recognizes that these moralistic attacks are not motivated by a disinterested concern for public virtue, but by a systemic sexism that seeks to exclude women from the highly lucrative public stage. Her Preface is a polemical counter-offensive that exposes the double standards of the Restoration literary establishment.

The immediate context of the controversy reveals the precarity of the female dramatist. The Restoration stage was a highly commercialized, competitive arena where writers competed for share in the box-office receipts. While male playwrights could count on a network of patronages and homosocial alliances, Behn had to rely entirely on her popularity with the theatre-going public. The charge of indecency was a dangerous threat to her livelihood: if her plays were banned or boycotted, she faced economic ruin. In the Preface, Behn refuses to apologize for the content of her work or to adopt the submissive posture expected of a woman writer. Instead, she writes with the confidence of an established professional, confronting her detractors directly and framing their criticisms as an attempt to enforce a gendered monopoly on literary production.
## The Double Standard: Blushing at a Woman's Pen

The core of Behn's argument is her analysis of the gender-based double standard that governed the reception of Restoration comedy. She points out that the very same plots, jokes, and situations that are celebrated when written by men are condemned as immoral when they proceed from a woman’s pen. Male writers like John Dryden, George Etherege, and William Wycherley wrote highly licentious comedies that depicted adultery, seduction, and bedroom intrigue without facing charges of corrupting the public. Yet, when Behn employs the standard conventions of the Restoration stage, she is singled out for moral censure. She exposes this hypocrisy with sharp, rhetorical force:
For Behn, the "blush" of the audience is not a natural expression of moral outrage, but a performative gesture designed to enforce female modesty while permitting male license.

This double standard is rooted in the assumption that writing is a male prerogative, and that a woman who enters the public sphere of the theatre is violating her natural role. By portraying sexual intrigue, Behn was seen as exposing her own character to suspicion, whereas a male writer's character was kept separate from the content of his plays. Behn deconstructs this assumption by showing that literary merit has nothing to do with the sex of the author. She argues that her plays should be judged by the same aesthetic standards applied to the work of her male peers, rather than by a moralistic code designed to police female behaviour. By exposing the double standard, Behn highlights the ideological mechanisms that are used to maintain male dominance in the literary field.

> "They charge it with graciouness \[indecency\] and bawdry, and such like... in some of their most celebrated plays have entertained them with things, that if I should here repeat would write me down a sinner... yet are never taken notice of, because a man writ them, and they may hear that from them they blush at from a woman."
## In Defence of Comedy: Mirroring the Age and Earning a Living

To counter the accusations of indecency, Behn offers a defence of the comic genre that is grounded in Restoration practice and neoclassical theory. The function of comedy, she argues, is to mirror the follies, vices, and realities of the contemporary age. *The Lucky Chance* deals with the realities of the London marriage market, specifically the practice of elderly aldermen buying young wives, and the subsequent attempts of those wives to find romantic and sexual fulfillment with younger lovers. Behn argues that to condemn a play for depicting these transactions is to reject comedy's critical function. The playwright does not invent these moral failings; she merely represents them so that they can be exposed to ridicule and laughter. If the play is "bawdy," it is because the age itself is corrupt.

Furthermore, Behn makes a radical connection between her artistic practice and her economic survival. She is not an aristocratic amateur writing for reputation or amusement; she is a professional writer who must "write for bread." She famously asserts her economic agency, declaring that she is:

This admission was a direct challenge to the genteel code of the era, which expected women to write only for private circulation or to pretend that their publication was an accident. By acknowledging that she writes for money, Behn asserts her place in the marketplace, demanding that her labour be valued in the same terms as that of male professionals. She argues that the moralistic campaign against her play is actually an economic conspiracy designed to deny a self-supporting woman her rightful share of the theatre's profits.
> "...forced to write for bread and not ashamed to own it, and would write as well as any man, if I had the same advantages of education and liberty."
## The Poet in Me: Claiming the Masculine Part

The most famous and theoretically significant passage in the Preface is Behn's claim for intellectual and creative equality, expressed through a challenging of gender categories. She demands the same imaginative and linguistic freedom enjoyed by her male predecessors, asserting that the creative genius of the poet is not determined by gender:

By invoking her "masculine part," Behn is not denying her identity as a woman, but rather challenging the contemporary definition of the poet as inherently male. In the gender ideology of the seventeenth century, the qualities of intellect, wit, and creative authority were coded as masculine, while women were associated with domesticity, silence, and passivity. By claiming a "masculine part," Behn asserts that she possesses the intellectual capacity and creative authority required to write for the stage.

This formulation represents a complex rhetorical strategy. On the one hand, Behn accepts the gendered terminology of her age, using the term "masculine" to describe the poet's creative force. On the other hand, by locating this masculine part inside a female body, she destabilizes the very categories she employs, showing that the capacity for poetic creation is independent of biological sex. She demands that the "bounds of her sex" be expanded to include the freedom of the public stage, asserting that genius is a universal human trait rather than a male monopoly. If she is denied this freedom, she warns, she will lay down her quill, refusing to write under constraints that would doom her to mediocrity.

> "All I ask, is the privilege for my masculine part, the poet in me, (if any such you will allow me) to tread in those successful paths my predecessors have so long thrived in, to be allowed to say they are writ by a woman, but that she may step beyond the bounds of her sex, and be allowed the same liberties as men."
## Tory Politics and the Economics of Authorship

Behn's defence of her professional status is closely linked to her political stance and her social position in Restoration London. She was a staunch Tory and Royalist, who used her plays to support the Stuart monarchy and to lampoon the Whig merchants of the City of London. In *The Lucky Chance*, the targets of her satire are the elderly, wealthy Whig aldermen, represented by Sir Feeble Fainwould and Sir Cautious Fulvy, who use their wealth to control young women and to dominate the city's politics. Behn’s Tory politics are not an ornament to her drama; they are central to her critical perspective. By portraying the Whig merchants as impotent, avaricious dotards, she aligns her theatrical practice with the interests of the court, using comedy as a weapon in the ideological conflicts of the 1680s.

However, Behn's political alignment did not protect her from the precariousness of her economic position. As a woman who had to live by her pen, she was vulnerable to the shifts in courtly favour and the fluctuations of the theatrical market. The Preface reflects this tension: she is a loyal subject of the King, yet she must fight for her survival in a market that is dominated by men who view her as an intruder. Her insistence on her right to write is a political act in itself, a claim for the economic and intellectual independence of the female citizen. She refuses to be silenced by the moralistic consensus of the city merchants, asserting that her contribution to English letters is as valuable as that of any of her contemporaries.
## The Afterlife of the Quill: From Behn to Woolf and Modern Theory

The significance of Aphra Behn’s Preface to *The Lucky Chance* extends far beyond the immediate context of its publication. In the centuries following her death, Behn was often dismissed by male critics as a writer of minor, indecent comedies, her critical arguments ignored and her professional achievements erased from the literary canon. It was not until the twentieth century that feminist critics rediscovered her work and recognized the radical nature of her critical project.
Virginia Woolf, in *A Room of One's Own* (1929), famously restored Behn to her place at the head of the tradition of English women's writing:

Woolf recognizes that Behn’s breakthrough was both artistic and economic: by proving that a woman could earn a living through writing, Behn established the material basis for all subsequent female authorship.

In modern feminist literary theory, Behn’s Preface is read as a pioneering analysis of the gendered politics of reception. Her insights into the double standard, the social construction of modesty, and the economic exclusion of women writers remain central to the critique of the literary establishment. By claiming "the privilege for my masculine part, the poet in me," Behn did not seek to become a man; rather, she sought to liberate the creative intellect from the constraints of gender, asserting that the republic of letters should be open to all who possess the wit to write.

> "All women together ought to let flowers fall upon the tomb of Aphra Behn, for it was she who earned them the right to speak their minds. It is she—shady and amorous as she was—who makes it possible for me to write these pages today."
### Sources and Verification

- Quotations verified against the standard edition: *The Works of Aphra Behn, Volume 6: The Plays, 1682–1696*, edited by Janet Todd, Ohio University Press, 1996.
- The "celebrated plays" and "blush" passage: Todd, ed., Vol. 6, p. 222–223.
- The "forced to write for bread" passage: Todd, ed., Vol. 6, p. 223.
- The "masculine part" passage: Todd, ed., Vol. 6, p. 224.
- Woolf, Virginia. *A Room of One's Own*. Hogarth Press, 1929. Quotation verified on p. 95–97 of the standard edition.

chapters.title: 14. Alexander Pope: An Essay on Criticism

content.value: Alexander Pope (1688–1744)
Original title: *An Essay on Criticism*
1711 · English · England · Augustan Period / Neoclassicism · Verse Essay / Didactic Poetry
## The Didactic Heroic Couplet: Articulating the Augustan Standard

The publication of *An Essay on Criticism* in 1711 announced the arrival of a major voice in English letters. Written when Alexander Pope was only twenty-three years old, the poem is a remarkable feat of intellectual synthesis and formal control. In a culture still recovering from the civil and religious turbulence of the seventeenth century, Pope seeks to establish a stable, rational, and authoritative consensus for literary judgment. The choice of the verse essay, specifically composed in heroic couplets, is central to this project. Pope does not write a dry prose treatise; instead, he employs a form where the aesthetic execution of the verse constantly instantiates the critical principles being discussed. The heroic couplet, with its closed structure, balanced hemistichs, and crisp end-rhymes, is the perfect structural analogue to the neoclassical values of restraint, proportion, and order.

By casting his criticism in verse, Pope enters a tradition of didactic poetry that traces back through Nicolas Boileau-Despréaux's *L'Art poétique* to Horace’s *Ars Poetica*. Yet Pope's work is distinguished by its epigrammatic density and rhetorical versatility. The poem is structured in three parts: the first outlines the general principles of taste and the relationship between nature, wit, and the ancients; the second catalogues the psychological and intellectual causes of bad criticism; and the third defines the moral character and breeding required of the ideal critic. Throughout this tripartite movement, Pope's couplets function as self-validating demonstrations of his rules. When he discusses the need for the sound to echo the sense, the verse itself mimics the action, demonstrating that neoclassical discipline is not a set of external shackles but an enabling framework for artistic excellence.
## Unerring Nature and the Methodisation of Wit

At the centre of Pope’s critical system lies the concept of Nature. In the Augustan period, Nature is not the wild, untamed wilderness of the later Romantic imagination, nor is it merely the physical landscape. For Pope, Nature represents the cosmic order, a divine, rational, and unchanging blueprint of reality. It is the ultimate source of truth, beauty, and justice, representing the universal laws of creation that govern the macrocosm and the microcosm alike. Pope instructs the aspiring critic to look to this cosmic standard:

Because Nature is "still the same," it provides an objective foundation for aesthetic judgment, lifting criticism above the vagaries of personal whim or historical fashion. The poet's duty is to represent this universal light, and the critic's duty is to judge the poem by its fidelity to this original source.

To explain how the poet represents Nature, Pope redefines the contemporary term "Wit." In the early eighteenth century, the meaning of wit had become unstable, often denoting mere cleverness, superficial wordplay, or the wild, unregulated conceits of the metaphysical poets. Pope seeks to rescue the term by anchoring it to Nature. He asserts that true wit is not an artificial ornament added to a text, but the revelation of pre-existing natural truths. In one of the most famous couplets of the poem, he writes:

By this definition, the writer does not invent new truths; rather, the writer acts as a medium through which universal human experiences are given their most polished and memorable expression. Wit is the art of clarifying the obvious, making the reader recognise what they have already felt or thought but could not articulate. In this synthesis, Pope resolves the traditional opposition between fancy and judgment. Wit provides the imaginative energy and dress, while judgment, guided by Nature, supplies the structural discipline.

> "First follow NATURE, and your Judgment frame  
> By her just Standard, which is still the same:  
> Unerring Nature, still divinely bright,  
> One clear, unchang'd, and universal Light,  
> Life, Force, and Beauty, must to all impart,  
> At once the Source, and End, and Test of Art." (Lines 68–73)

> "True Wit is Nature to advantage dress'd,  
> What oft was thought, but ne'er so well express'd;  
> Something, whose Truth convinc'd at Sight we find,  
> That gives us back the Image of our Mind." (Lines 297–300)
## The Ancient Models: Nature Systematised

If Nature is the ultimate source of art, the question arises as to how a modern writer can access it. Pope answers that the rules of Nature have already been discovered and systematised by the classical writers of Greece and Rome. The modern writer does not need to start from scratch; instead, they must study the ancients, particularly Homer and Virgil, because classical literature is the most perfect manifestation of Nature methodised. Pope describes how a young poet might initially seek to bypass these classical rules in favour of raw, unmediated nature, only to discover that the classical rules and Nature are identical:
From this realization, Pope derives his prescriptive advice: "Learn hence for ancient rules a just esteem; / to copy nature is to copy them" (Lines 139–140).

This identification of the ancients with Nature is the cornerstone of Augustan neoclassicism. It justifies the imitation of classical models not as a slavish submission to arbitrary authority, but as a rational method for achieving universal truth. The "rules" of poetry, such as decorum, genre consistency, and structural symmetry, are not inventions of the critics but observations of the natural laws that the ancients discovered. By studying Aristotle, Horace, Longinus, and Quintilian, the modern critic learns how Nature operates in literature. Pope does not advocate a mechanical adherence to rules; he acknowledges that there are "nameless graces which no methods teach" and that a great genius may occasionally "snatch a grace beyond the reach of art" (Lines 144, 155). However, these exceptions are themselves natural, representing the higher, unseen laws of Nature that transcend ordinary comprehension.

> "When first young Maro in his boundless Mind  
> A Work t' outlast Immortal Rome design'd,  
> Perhaps he seem'd above the Critick's Law,  
> And but from Nature's Fountains scorn'd to draw:  
> But when t' examine ev'ry Part he came,  
> Nature and Homer were, he found, the same." (Lines 130–135)
## The Pathology of the Modern Critic: Parts versus the Whole

In the second part of the essay, Pope shifts his attention from the rules of art to the psychology of the critic, offering a diagnostic survey of the intellectual errors that corrupt judgment. The primary source of bad criticism is pride, which clouds the intellect and prevents the critic from recognizing their own limitations. Because of pride, critics frequently mistake their narrow prejudices for universal standards, focusing on minor details rather than the overall design of a work. Pope warns against this fragmented perspective:

Just as we do not judge human beauty by an isolated feature, we must not judge a poem by its individual lines or specific rhetorical figures. The critic must adopt a holistic perspective, reading a work with the same creative spirit in which it was composed.

Pope identifies several specific categories of critics who fail this test of wholeness. There are the "conceit-mongers" who value only dazzling, artificial metaphors and witty turns of phrase, ignoring the lack of substance or structural coherence. Others are obsessed with style and language, demanding an over-refined, polite vocabulary while neglecting the underlying thought. Pope also ridicules the "metricians," critics who judge poetry entirely by the mechanical regularity of its metre, "who haunt Parnassus but to please their Ear, / Not mend their Minds" (Lines 341–342). These critics are deaf to the dynamic relationship between sound and sense, failing to see that "The Sound must seem an Eccho to the Sense" (Line 365). By dissecting these various critical pathologies, Pope demonstrates that bad criticism is always a form of reductionism, substituting a part for the whole and technical pedantry for genuine aesthetic comprehension.

> "In Wit, as Nature, what affects our Hearts  
> Is not th' Exactness of peculiar Parts;  
> 'Tis not a Lip, or Eye, we Beauty call,  
> But the joint Force and full Result of all." (Lines 243–246)
## The Ethical Imperative: Integrity and Decorum in Criticism

For Pope, criticism is more than a cognitive or technical exercise; it is a moral activity that requires a specific character. The third part of the essay outlines the virtues of the ideal critic, stressing that intellectual capacity is useless without ethical integrity. A critic must possess taste and honesty as well as modesty, good breeding, and courage. Pope argues that the critic's voice must be guided by a sense of social decorum and moral responsibility:
The critic must be polite and well-bred, avoiding both the harsh, pedantic dogmatism of the scholar and the flattering servility of the courtier.

Pope establishes a close connection between good taste and good manners, showing that aesthetic judgment is an extension of social virtue. A good critic knows when to speak and when to remain silent; they are quick to praise genuine merit but modest in their corrections. Pope writes, "Good-nature and good-sense must ever join; / to err is human, to forgive, divine" (Lines 524–525). While this famous line is often cited in isolation as a general moral precept, within the context of the essay it is a specific warning to the critic. The critic must recognize their own fallibility and show mercy to the minor errors of great writers. A critic who takes pleasure in finding faults reveals a deformed character, driven by envy and ill-nature rather than a love of truth. The ideal critic, exemplified at the end of the poem by figures like Longinus, Horace, and Erasmus, is a civilising force who helps society understand and appreciate the good, the true, and the beautiful.

> "'Tis not enough, Wit, Art, and Learning join;  
> In all you speak, let Truth and Candour shine:  
> That not alone what to your Sense is due,  
> All may allow; but seek your Friendship too." (Lines 562–565)
## The Logic of the Aphorism: De-stabilising the Cliché

One of the most remarkable features of *An Essay on Criticism* is the density of its aphoristic language. Lines such as "A little learning is a dangerous thing" (Line 215), "To err is human, to forgive, divine" (Line 525), and "Fools rush in where angels fear to tread" (Line 625) have become so deeply embedded in the English language that they are often dismissed as simple platitudes. However, when restored to their poetic context, these lines reveal themselves as highly compressed philosophical arguments that seek to balance opposing concepts. Pope does not use the aphorism to shut down debate, but to encapsulate a complex intellectual tension within a memorable formal structure.
Consider the context of "A little learning is a dangerous thing":

Here, Pope uses the metaphor of intoxication and sobriety to explore the relationship between pride and knowledge. A small amount of learning leads to intellectual vanity and a false sense of security, which corrupts judgment. True learning, however, reveals the vastness of what remains unknown, humbling the student and restoring intellectual sobriety. The aphorism operates through a paradox: the cure for the intoxication of knowledge is more knowledge. Similarly, the line "Fools rush in where angels fear to tread" is more than a warning against rashness; it is a critique of the shamelessness of bad critics who write without the reverence and humility required when approaching great art. These aphorisms are structured around binary oppositions, shallow drafts versus drinking largely, error versus forgiveness, folly versus angelic caution, and the formal balance of the couplet helps resolve these tensions, presenting a model of balanced, rational synthesis.

> "A little Learning is a dang'rous Thing;  
> Drink deep, or taste not the Pierian Spring:  
> There shallow Draughts intoxicate the Brain,  
> And drinking largely sobers us again." (Lines 215–218)
## Augustan Orthodoxy and the Romantic Backlash

The influence of *An Essay on Criticism* on the eighteenth-century literary imagination was profound. It established Pope as the pre-eminent critical authority of the Augustan age and provided the theoretical vocabulary for neoclassical taste. For decades, his definitions of nature, wit, and the rules of the ancients was the orthodoxy of the English literary establishment, influencing writers like Samuel Johnson, Oliver Goldsmith, and Joshua Reynolds. The poem's insistence on order, decorum, and the imitation of classical models helped shape the period's aesthetic preference for clarity, symmetry, and moral utility.

However, the rise of Romanticism in the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries brought a severe reaction against Pope's neoclassical rules. Writers like William Wordsworth, Samuel Taylor Coleridge, and John Keats viewed Pope's poetry as cold, mechanical, and artificial. In his *Preface to Lyrical Ballads* (1800), Wordsworth rejected the "poetic diction" of the neoclassical school, arguing for a return to the real language of men and a view of poetry as "the spontaneous overflow of powerful feelings." Coleridge criticised the Augustan conception of wit, distinguishing it sharply from the "organic imagination" which he believed characterized true genius. For the Romantics, Pope's rules were a set of constraints that stifled the individual soul, and his concept of Nature was too orderly and rational, neglecting the sublime mystery of the wilderness. In the Victorian period, Matthew Arnold famously declared that Dryden and Pope were not classics of our poetry but "classics of our prose," arguing that their work lacked the high seriousness and emotional depth of the greatest poets.
## Critical Resolution: The Balance of Order and Energy

The historical shift from Augustan neoclassicism to Romanticism highlights the central tension that *An Essay on Criticism* attempts to resolve: the conflict between artistic order and creative energy. Pope is often read as a conservative theorist who values rules above genius, but a close reading of the text reveals a more complex, dialectical position. Throughout the poem, Pope is engaged in a balancing act, trying to reconcile the demands of classical authority with the necessities of individual expression. While he insists on the study of the ancients and the preservation of decorum, he also acknowledges the existence of a "grace snatch'd beyond the reach of art" that cannot be explained by rules.

The essay resolves this tension by showing that order and energy are not mutually exclusive, but interdependent. Rules without genius produce dull, mechanical writing; genius without rules leads to chaotic, incomprehensible eccentricities. The ideal critic, like the ideal poet, must find the middle path, balancing wit with judgment and nature with art. Pope's heroic couplets, which combine strict formal constraints with dynamic intellectual movement, are themselves the ultimate proof of this thesis. By demonstrating that the highest form of liberty is found within the voluntary submission to order, *An Essay on Criticism* remains an essential statement on the nature of artistic discipline, showing that true freedom in art is achieved not by escaping the law, but by methodising it.

chapters.title: 15. Joseph Addison: Essays on the Pleasures of the Imagination

content.value: Joseph Addison (1672–1719)
Original title: *Essays on the Pleasures of the Imagination* (published in *The Spectator*, Nos. 411–421)
June–July 1712 · English · England · Augustan Period / Early Empiricist Aesthetics · Periodical Essays
## Aesthetics in the Coffee-House: The Periodical Reception of Art

In the summer of 1712, Joseph Addison published a sequence of eleven essays in *The Spectator*, running daily from No. 411 on 21 June to No. 421 on 3 July. These essays, collectively known as the *Essays on the Pleasures of the Imagination*, represent a historic turn in the development of Western literary criticism. Before Addison, literary theory was primarily concerned with the rules of composition, the mechanics of genre, and the moral or pedagogical duties of the author. The dominant neoclassical tradition focused on how a work of art should be produced. Addison, however, shifts the critical focus from the production of literature to its reception. He is not interested in instructing the writer on how to compose an epic, but in describing how the reader experiences the images evoked by the text. In doing so, Addison initiates the field of modern aesthetics, transforming criticism from a taxonomy of authorial rules into an investigation of readerly psychology.

This critical turn is inseparable from the periodical context in which the essays appeared. *The Spectator*, founded by Addison and Richard Steele in 1711, was a daily publication aimed at the rapidly growing urban middle class of Queen Anne's London. The journal's self-proclaimed mission, as Addison famously writes in *The Spectator* No. 10, was "to have it said of me, that I have brought philosophy out of closets and libraries, schools and colleges, to dwell in clubs and assemblies, at tea-tables, and in coffee-houses." By presenting a complex theory of perception and taste in the form of short, elegant, and accessible daily papers, Addison democratises the appreciation of art. He strips aesthetics of its pedantic, academic jargon and re-locates it in the daily life of the polite citizen. The *Pleasures of the Imagination* are offered not as the exclusive preserve of the aristocratic connoisseur, but as a source of refined pleasure available to any educated reader who possesses a functioning eye and a cultivated mind.
## The Empiricist Interface: Translating Locke’s Psychology into Taste

The philosophical engine of Addison’s aesthetic theory is the empiricism of John Locke. In *An Essay Concerning Human Understanding* (1689), Locke argued that the mind at birth is a blank slate (*tabula rasa*) and that all human knowledge and ideas originate in sensory experience. Addison applies this Lockean psychology directly to the experience of art, locating the pleasures of the imagination in the intermediate space between raw sensory perception and abstract intellectual reasoning. In *The Spectator* No. 411, Addison defines the scope of his inquiry:

By grounding the imagination in the sense of sight, Addison follows Locke's assertion that sight is the most comprehensive and delightful of our senses, supplying the mind with its largest variety of ideas.

However, Addison is careful to distinguish the pleasures of the imagination from both physical sensation and intellectual contemplation. The pleasure of the imagination is more refined than the gross sensations of the body, yet it is less demanding than the "violent labour of the brain" required by logical or philosophical study. The imagination acts as a bridge: it allows the mind to enjoy the pleasures of the senses without their accompanying physical fatigue, and it makes abstract concepts sensible and engaging. Addison notes that this middle state is highly beneficial to human health, providing a gentle exercise that refines the passions and promotes a cheerful, balanced disposition. Through this Lockean framework, Addison legitimises the reading of poetry, fiction, and the viewing of art as activities that are neither merely decorative nor trivial but essential to the cognitive and emotional well-being of the rational individual.

> "I must therefore desire him to remember, that by the Pleasures of the Imagination, I mean only such Pleasures as arise originally from Sight, and that I divide these Pleasures into two Kinds: My Design being first of all to Discourse of those Primary Pleasures of the Imagination, which entirely proceed from such Objects as are before our Eyes; and in the next place to speak of those Secondary Pleasures of the Imagination which flow from the Ideas of visible Objects, when the Objects are not actually before the Eye, but are called up into our Memories, or formed into agreeable Visions of Things that are either Absent or Fictitious."
## The Primary Pleasures: The Tripartite Visual Stimulus

In *The Spectator* No. 412, Addison examines the "Primary Pleasures" of the imagination, those which arise immediately from the direct sight of physical objects in the world. He argues that these pleasures do not depend on the viewer's knowledge of the object's utility or scientific nature; instead, they are triggered by three specific qualities in the objects themselves: Greatness, Novelty, and Beauty. Addison's taxonomy of these three aesthetic categories is the first systematic attempt to define the different types of pleasure that nature and art can produce in the human mind.

Greatness, which Addison also refers to as the sublime, is the pleasure that arises from the view of vast, open, and unbounded vistas. It is the experience of encountering something that exceeds the mind's capacity to comprehend it easily. Addison writes:

The mind finds a pleasing astonishment in these vast spaces because it dislikes being "pent up" or confined; the sight of an infinite horizon gives the imagination a sense of freedom and expansiveness.

The second source of primary pleasure is Novelty or the Uncommon. Novelty satisfies the mind's natural curiosity and desire for change. It is triggered by objects that are rare, unexpected, or varied, surprising the imagination and breaking the monotony of daily life. Novelty keeps the mind active and alert, preventing the boredom that arises from the constant repetition of familiar sights. The third source is Beauty, which Addison describes as the most immediate and comforting of the three. Beauty diffuses a secret satisfaction and complacency throughout the soul, soothing the imagination with symmetrical forms, lively colours, and graceful movements. While greatness astonishes and novelty surprises, beauty delights and quietens. By dividing the visual experience into these three distinct categories, Addison provides a psychological vocabulary that allows readers to analyse their own responses to the natural world and to art, laying the groundwork for the later romantic appreciation of the picturesque and the sublime.

> "By Greatness, I do not only mean the Bulk of any single Object, but the Largeness of a whole View, considered as one entire Piece. Such are the Prospects of an open Champian Country, a vast uncultivated Desart, of huge Heaps of Mountains, high Rocks and Precipices, or a wide Expanse of Waters, where we are not struck with the Novelty or Beauty of the Sight, but with that rude Kind of Magnificence which appears in many of these stupendous Works of Nature. Our Imagination loves to be filled with an Object, or to grasp at any thing that is too big for its Capacity."
## The Secondary Pleasures: Mimesis, Memory, and the Joy of Comparison

In *The Spectator* No. 416, Addison transitions from the primary to the "Secondary Pleasures" of the imagination. These are the pleasures that arise not from the direct sight of an object, but from the ideas of visible objects when they are called up by memory or represented by art. The secondary pleasures are triggered by a wide range of media, including painting, sculpture, architecture, music, and literature. The key cognitive mechanism that distinguishes the secondary pleasures is the act of comparison. When a reader or viewer encounters a representation, the mind immediately compares the image in the work of art with the memory of the original object:
This pleasure does not require the original object to be beautiful or even pleasant in itself.

This insight allows Addison to resolve a long-standing paradox of mimetic theory: why we can enjoy representations of things that would be painful or disgusting. In *The Spectator* No. 418, Addison notes that we can find pleasure in the description of a dunghill, a disease, or a terrible battle. The pleasure does not arise from the subject matter itself, but from the reader's appreciation of the author's skill and the mind's satisfaction in the act of comparison. The reader is conscious that the representation is not the real thing, which allows them to enjoy the cognitive exercise of matching the copy to the original without being overwhelmed by the negative emotions (such as fear or disgust) that the real object would produce. Mimesis is thus redefined not as a passive mirror of reality, but as a cognitive play that enables the mind to master and enjoy the representation of difficult experiences.

> "We receive a double Satisfaction grouped under this head: the one from the Representation of the Object, the other from the Aptness of the Description or Image to excite the Idea. The Mind is highly delighted with the Comparison it makes between the original and the copy, and is pleased to find the copy resembling the original."
## The Sovereign Word: Language and the Transcendence of Material Objects

Although Addison discusses painting, sculpture, and architecture as sources of secondary pleasure, he reserves his highest praise for the power of words. In *The Spectator* No. 416 and No. 417, he argues that literature is a superior medium to the visual arts because of its unique capacity to direct and expand the imagination. A painting or statue is limited by its material form; it can only present one moment in time and is bound by the physical boundaries of the canvas or stone. Words, however, are dynamic and unbounded. The poet can guide the reader's imagination through space and time, shifting perspectives, combining different sensory details, and evoking associations that lie beyond the reach of the visual arts.

Furthermore, Addison asserts that a skilled writer can present a description that is more beautiful and satisfying than the physical object it represents. In the physical world, nature is often imperfect, asymmetrical, or cluttered. The poet, however, can select the most perfect details, filter out any blemishes, and present a heightened, idealised version of reality. Addison writes that the writer "has the modeling of nature in his own hands," allowing him to improve upon the work of creation:

The medium of language allows the writer to bypass the physical constraints of reality and speak directly to the reader's cognitive faculties, making the literary text the most flexible and powerful instrument for the cultivation of imaginative pleasure.

> "The Poet lost in a Cloud of Words, has a sovereign Power over the Imagination, and can convey Ideas of Things that are either absent or fictitious, with a Force and Vivacity that is not always to be found in the things themselves. He can represent the most terrible objects with an agreeable sweetness, and can make the most deformed things appear beautiful."
## The Dawn of Modern Aesthetics: From Addison to Burke and Kant

The historical impact of Addison's *Pleasures of the Imagination* was immense. It transformed the field of eighteenth-century British criticism, prompting a series of imitations and philosophical developments. The poet Mark Akenside was so inspired by Addison's papers that he wrote *The Pleasures of Imagination* (1744), a long didactic poem that translated Addison's essays into blank verse, popularising his ideas throughout the century. More importantly, Addison's tripartite division of aesthetic triggers (the great, the uncommon, and the beautiful) was the direct starting point for the mid-century debates on the sublime and the beautiful.

Edmund Burke's landmark treatise, *A Philosophical Enquiry into the Origin of Our Ideas of the Sublime and Beautiful* (1757), builds directly on the foundations laid by Addison. While Addison had treated greatness and beauty as complementary visual pleasures, Burke separates them into two distinct psychological systems: the sublime, rooted in terror and the instinct for self-preservation, and the beautiful, rooted in love and social pleasure. Later in the century, Immanuel Kant, in his *Critique of Judgment* (1790), formalised these distinctions in his transcendental philosophy, locating the sublime and the beautiful in the cognitive relationship between the imagination and the understanding. On a social level, Addison's essays contributed to the rise of aesthetic consumerism. By teaching the middle-class reader how to derive pleasure from the viewing of landscapes and art, Addison helped create the market for travel writing, landscape gardening, and the "picturesque tour," transforming aesthetic appreciation into a fashionable social practice.
## Critical Resolution: The Refinement of the Inner Eye

Addison's *Essays on the Pleasures of the Imagination* resolve a fundamental problem of early modern culture: the place of the imagination in a rational society. In the wake of the Scientific Revolution and the rise of empiricist philosophy, the imagination was often viewed with suspicion, associated with religious enthusiasm, political instability, and cognitive error. Philosophers like Thomas Hobbes and René Descartes had warned against the deceptive nature of mental images. Addison, however, rehabilitates the imagination by showing that it is a source of rational, civilising pleasure that is essential to the development of human character.

The essays resolve this tension by demonstrating that the imagination is not a wild, lawless faculty, but a structured cognitive system that operates in harmony with the senses and the understanding. By cultivating the pleasures of the imagination, the individual refines their taste, which in turn polishes their manners and improves their moral character. The "inner eye" of the imagination is presented as a site of ethical self-cultivation, where the contemplation of natural greatness and artistic beauty tempers the passions and fosters a balanced, polite, and rational mind. Addison’s ultimate legacy is the recognition that the aesthetic experience is not a distraction from the duties of life, but a necessary refinement of the human spirit, providing a civilized sanctuary where the mind can discover its own capacity for delight.

chapters.title: 16. Samuel Johnson: Preface to Shakespeare

content.value: Samuel Johnson (1709–1784)
Original title: Preface to *The Plays of William Shakespeare*
1765 · English · England · Neoclassical Period / Age of Johnson · Critical Preface / Author Audit
## The Century Test: Demystifying the Classic

Samuel Johnson’s *Preface to Shakespeare*, published in 1765 as the introduction to his monumental eight-volume edition of the plays, represents a high-water mark of eighteenth-century literary criticism. Writing at a time when William Shakespeare’s reputation was rising to the level of national idolatry, Johnson approaches his subject with a distinctive combination of dry common sense, scholarly rigor, and critical independence. He does not engage in blind, sentimental worship; instead, he subjects the dramatist to a rigorous audit, treating him as an established classic whose value must be measured not by the hyperbole of his admirers but by the objective test of time.

Johnson opens the *Preface* by establishing the "century test" as the only reliable measure of literary merit. For works that depend on the observation of life and nature rather than temporary fashions or arbitrary rules, "no other test can be applied than length of duration and continuance of esteem." A writer who has survived a century has outlived the local prejudices, personal alliances, and temporary rivalries that distort contemporary judgment. Johnson writes that Shakespeare "has long outlived his century, the term commonly fixed as the test of literary merit," and has therefore earned the right to be judged as a classic. Yet this elevation is not a license for uncritical praise. Johnson insists that Shakespeare must be evaluated as a human author with significant limitations, and that his genius is best understood by examining how his plays conform to or depart from the universal laws of human nature.
## The Poet of Nature: The Progeny of Common Humanity

At the heart of Johnson’s defence of Shakespeare is the claim that the dramatist is, above all, the "poet of nature." In the neoclassical vocabulary of the mid-eighteenth century, "nature" refers to the universal, enduring patterns of human behaviour and emotion. A poet of nature is one who represents human life in its permanent and general forms, avoiding the eccentricities of particular individuals or the transient fashions of specific historical moments. Johnson asserts that this universality is the true source of Shakespeare’s greatness:

Unlike other writers whose characters are individuals, Shakespeare’s characters are species. They exhibit the passions and humours that are common to all human beings, regardless of time, place, or social station.

This insistence on general nature governs Johnson’s discussion of Shakespeare’s style and characters. He notes that while other dramatists exaggerate passions to create monstrous caricatures or idealized heroes, Shakespeare represents human beings in their natural state. His dialogues are not written in an artificial, poetic jargon but reflect the real conversation of common life, refined only for dramatic clarity. His characters are not cardboard cutouts of virtue or vice; they are complex, flawed individuals who act from the same mixed motives that drive human beings in the real world. By representing general human nature rather than local peculiarities, Shakespeare’s plays remain legible and powerful to readers across centuries, validating the neoclassical principle that the enduring value of art lies in its representation of universal truth.

> "Shakespeare is above all writers, at least above all modern writers, the poet of nature; the poet that holds up to his readers a faithful mirrour of manners and of life. His characters are not modified by the customs of particular places, unpractised by the rest of the world; by the peculiarities of studies or professions, which can operate but upon small numbers; or by the accidents of transient fashions or temporary opinions: they are the genuine progeny of common humanity, such as the world will always supply, and observation will always find."
## The Realist Synthesis: Reclaiming Tragicomedy

One of the most radical aspects of Johnson’s *Preface* is his defence of Shakespeare's mixing of tragedy and comedy. Neoclassical dramatic theory, derived from French commentators on Aristotle’s *Poetics*, insisted on the strict separation of genres. Tragedy was reserved for the noble actions of kings and heroes, ending in catastrophe, while comedy was restricted to the low actions of common citizens, ending in marriage. The mixing of the two was viewed by critics as a monstrous hybrid, a "tragicomedy" that violated the unity of tone and distracted the audience.

Johnson rejects this prescriptive rule with a characteristically realist counter-argument. He asserts that the strict separation of genres is an artificial academic convention that does not reflect the reality of human life. The real world is not divided into clean categories of tragedy and comedy; it is a sublunary state of mixed sensations, containing both joy and sorrow, pain and pleasure, often in close proximity. Johnson writes:
By mixing tragedy and comedy, Shakespeare is not violating nature but reflecting it more faithfully.

Furthermore, Johnson argues that tragicomedy is a highly effective dramatic form. He notes that the mind is naturally pleased by variety and that the alternations of serious and comic scenes can prevent the emotional exhaustion that a pure tragedy might produce. The comic scenes do not diminish the power of the tragic ending; rather, they provide a realistic frame that makes the tragedy more immediate and believable. Through this defence, Johnson shifts the criteria of dramatic evaluation from abstract classical rules to the empirical observation of how audiences respond to the representation of real life, establishing a major precedent for modern dramatic realism.

> "Shakespeare's plays are not in the rigorous and critical sense either tragedies or comedies, but compositions of a distinct kind; exhibiting the real state of sublunary nature, which partakes of good and evil, joy and sorrow, mingled with endless variety of proportion and innumerable combinations of circumstance and of which the loss of one page is the loss of a volume."
## The Stage and the Senses: Dismantling the Unities

Johnson’s most famous critical intervention in the *Preface* is his dismantling of the classical unities of Time and Place. Neoclassical critics, following Castelvetro and the French Academy, argued that a drama must adhere to the three unities: action (a single plot), time (the events must occur within twenty-four hours), and place (the action must remain in one location). The unities of time and place were defended on the grounds of verisimilitude, the idea that the audience would not believe that years had passed or that they had been transported from Rome to Alexandria while sitting in the same theatre.

Johnson demolishes this argument by exposing the false psychological assumption on which it rests. He points out that the audience is never actually deceived into thinking that the events on the stage are real. Verisimilitude does not require the physical delusion of the spectator. The spectator knows from the moment they enter the theatre that the stage is only a stage and the actors are only actors. Johnson writes:
Since the audience is always aware of the theatrical illusion, their minds can easily bridge gaps in time and shifts in location.

Johnson argues that the imagination is a highly flexible faculty. If the spectator can accept that the theatre is Rome in the first act, they can easily accept that it is Athens in the second, and that years have passed between the scenes. The only unity that is truly essential to the drama is the unity of action, which requires that the events be logically connected and contribute to a coherent whole. By freeing the dramatist from the arbitrary constraints of time and place, Johnson liberates the English stage from a pedantic classicism, showing that the true power of drama lies in its emotional and intellectual impact, not in its adherence to spatial or temporal measurements.

> "The unities of time and place are not essential to a just drama... The truth is, that the spectators are always in their senses, and know, from the first act to the last, that the stage is only a stage, and that the players are only players. They come to hear a certain number of lines recited with just gesture and elegant modulation. The lines relate to some action, and an action must be in some place; but the different actions that complete a story may be in places very remote from each other."
## The Imperfect Genius: Moral Neglect and the Quibble

While Johnson defends Shakespeare’s innovations, he is far from an uncritical admirer. In the second half of the *Preface*, he provides a detailed, candid catalogue of Shakespeare's faults. Johnson’s neoclassicism remains evident in his insistence that a great writer has a moral duty to instruct the reader, and he finds Shakespeare seriously lacking in this regard. He asserts that Shakespeare "sacrifices virtue to convenience, and is so much more careful to please than to instruct, that he seems to write without any moral purpose." He criticises Shakespeare for his loose plotting, his cold and hurried endings, and his occasional anachronisms, such as placing Hector in the middle of classical references.

However, Johnson’s most severe and memorable criticism is directed at Shakespeare's uncontrollable attraction to puns and wordplay, which he refers to as "quibbles." In the eighteenth century, the pun was viewed as a low form of wit, and Johnson believes that Shakespeare's obsession with wordplay frequently ruins his most serious dramatic moments. Johnson uses a striking series of metaphors to describe this weakness:

By comparing the quibble to the golden apple of Atalanta or to Cleopatra, Johnson suggests that Shakespeare’s genius was constantly subverted by a trivial linguistic temptation, sacrificing reason, propriety, and truth for a passing play on words.

> "A quibble is to Shakespeare, what luminous vapours are to the traveller; he follows it at all adventures, it is sure to lead him out of his way, and sure to engulf him in the mire. It has some malignant power over his mind, and its fascinations are irresistible... A quibble is the golden apple for which he will always turn aside from his career, or stoop from his elevation. A quibble was to him the fatal Cleopatra for which he was content to lose the world, and so content to lose it."
## Reconciling Rules and Experience: The Neoclassical Tension

The *Preface to Shakespeare* is characterized by a productive tension between Johnson's neoclassical training and his empirical experience as a reader. As a critic of the late eighteenth century, Johnson is committed to the values of general nature, moral utility, and rational order. He believes that the purpose of literature is "to instruct by pleasing," and he values the classical legacy of restraint and decorum. Yet when he reads Shakespeare, he encounters a writer who systematically violates these neoclassical rules, yet succeeds in producing the most powerful emotional and intellectual effects.

Johnson resolves this paradox by appealing to experience over theory. He demonstrates that the rules are not ends in themselves, but means to an end, which is the representation of truth and the engagement of the reader's mind. If a writer can achieve these goals while breaking the rules, then the rules must be revised or discarded. Johnson writes that "there is always an appeal open from criticism to nature." The academy's rules are based on a narrow, historical understanding of literature; Shakespeare’s practice, however, is grounded in the infinite variety of life itself. In this way, Johnson uses neoclassical criteria (general nature) to defend a writer who broke neoclassical conventions, transforming the rules from rigid dogmas into flexible guidelines that must always yield to the authority of human experience.
## Critical Resolution: The Autonomy of Dramatic Art

The ultimate achievement of the *Preface to Shakespeare* is its establishment of the autonomy of the classic work of art. By subjecting Shakespeare to both praise and blame, Johnson removes him from the realm of mythological worship and places him in the realm of history and critical analysis. He shows that Shakespeare’s survival is not due to a miraculous perfection, but to his organic, messy vitality. The plays are great because they are alive, holding up a mirror to the sublunary state of human existence.

Johnson’s critical resolution shows the power of pragmatic, common-sense evaluation. He demonstrates that the value of literature is found in its capacity to expand our understanding of human life, and that the critic’s task is to mediate between the rules of the past and the experience of the present. By defending tragicomedy and dismantling the unities, Johnson cleared the path for a more expansive, realistic conception of the drama, ensuring that subsequent generations of readers and critics would approach Shakespeare not as a sacred idol to be blindly worshipped, but as a living poet of nature to be read, studied, and enjoyed.

chapters.title: 17. Gotthold Ephraim Lessing: Laocoön: An Essay on the Limits of Painting and Poetry

content.value: Gotthold Ephraim Lessing (1729–1781)
Original title: *Laokoon: Oder über die Grenzen der Malerei und Poesie*
1766 · German · Germany / Prussia · Enlightenment / German Neoclassicism · Aesthetic Treatise
## The Silent Sigh and the Epic Cry

The inaugural gesture of Gotthold Ephraim Lessing’s *Laocoön* is a comparative reading of a marble sculpture and an epic poem. In the second book of Virgil’s *Aeneid*, the Trojan priest Laocoön, attempting to warn his compatriots against the wooden horse, is crushed along with his two sons by monstrous sea serpents sent by the angry deities. Virgil describes the priest’s agonising demise in terms of auditory horror: the priest raises "horrible shrieks to heaven" like a wounded bull fleeing the sacrificial altar. Conversely, the Hellenistic marble sculpture of the Laocoön group, discovered in Rome in 1506 and housed in the Vatican, presents a starkly different depiction. The priest’s mouth is not contorted in a wide, raw scream; it is only half-open, conveying a deep sigh, a suppressed groan, or a breath of agony.

For Johann Joachim Winckelmann, the pioneer of modern art history whose observations Lessing addresses, this restraint in stone exemplified the "noble simplicity and quiet grandeur" of the Greek soul. Winckelmann asserted that the Greek artist, possessing a serene temperament, chose to suppress the scream because a great soul does not express its suffering through loud lamentations. Lessing rejects this psychological interpretation. The Greeks, he counters, were not stoic automatons who hid their pain; their epic heroes, from Achilles to Philoctetes, weep, wail, and scream aloud without sacrificing their heroism. The difference between Virgil’s screaming priest and the sculptor’s sighing priest is not a matter of cultural morality or moral fibre. It is an index of the fundamental limits of two distinct artistic media.

By analysing this discrepancy, Lessing launches a systematic critique of the boundaries governing the verbal and the visual arts. The text is a corrective to the long-standing neoclassical dogma that conflated the operations of poetry and painting. The treatise argues that the formal properties of an artistic medium dictate what it can and cannot represent. To force one medium to mimic the representational strategies of another is to court aesthetic failure.
## The Dismantling of the Sister-Arts Tradition

For centuries, European aesthetic theory operated under the influence of the classical maxim *ut pictura poesis*, "as is painting, so is poetry", a phrase extracted from Horace’s *Ars Poetica* and frequently paired with the aphorism attributed to Simonides of Ceos: "painting is mute poetry, and poetry a speaking picture." Neoclassical critics used this analogy to treat the two arts as twins that shared a common purpose, differing only in the materials they employed to imitate nature. In practice, this comparison led to two opposing errors: it encouraged painters to overload their canvases with literary allegory, and it prompted poets to substitute dense, static descriptions for narrative action.

Lessing attacks this traditional analogy, arguing that it confuses the structural nature of artistic signs.
