In the legal system, for example, justice is not a matter of human empathy, but of the recursive application of legal codes. Similarly, in the literary system, meaning is generated not by the author's biography, but by the structural relations between texts. This shift from the individual to the system allows us to analyse complex social processes without relying on the humanist myth of the rational, self-determining agent, showing that social structures are non-human assemblages that operate according to their own internal logics.

Wolfe uses this systems-theoretic framework to analyse human subjectivity as a "strange loop." The human mind is not an autonomous, transparent source of meaning that stands outside the world, as Cartesian philosophy asserts. Rather, it is a closed, autopoietic system that is structurally coupled with its biological body and its technological environment. The subject is always-already dependent on non-human systems of communication, language, and technology to generate thought. Subjectivity is not a pure, internal essence; it is an emergent property that arises from our integration into these larger, self-referential networks. By combining Luhmann’s systems theory with Derrida’s deconstruction, Wolfe de-centres the sovereign individual, showing that meaning is not produced by a human actor, but is recursively generated through the complex interactions of autopoietic systems.
## Prosthetic Hybridity: The Human as a Technological Assemblage

A key posthumanist insight developed in *What is Posthumanism?* is the concept of prosthetic hybridity. Humanism has historically defined the human by distinguishing it from technology, treating tools as external instruments that the human rational mind manipulates. Wolfe challenges this division, arguing that the human is always-already coupled with technology. From the development of language and writing to the use of modern digital interfaces, technology is not an external supplement to the human; it is the very medium through which the human emerges.

Wolfe conceptualises the human as a technological assemblage, a hybrid entity that is constituted by both organic biology and inorganic prostheses. Our cognitive processes, our physical capacities, and our forms of communication are all mediated by non-human technologies. This prosthetic hybridity means that we cannot draw a clean line between the natural and the artificial, the biological and the mechanical. By showing that the human has never been autonomous, but has always depended on technological supplements for its existence, Wolfe deconstructs the humanist fantasy of self-sufficiency. The posthumanist subject is a hybrid creature, open to the world and embedded in a network of non-human actors, demonstrating that our relation to technology is not one of mastery, but of co-evolution.
## Posthumanist Ethics: Shared Vulnerability and Trans-Species Justice

The ultimate ambition of Wolfe’s monograph is to formulate a posthumanist ethics that can address the ecological and political crises of the twenty-first century. Traditional humanist ethics is based on the possession of reason, autonomy, and active agency. This framework is structurally incapable of addressing the needs of non-human animals, disabled humans, or ecosystems, all of which are excluded from the category of rational moral actors.

In contrast, Wolfe proposes a posthumanist ethics based on shared vulnerability, passivity, and finitude. Drawing on Derrida’s later writings on the animal, Wolfe argues that our ethical responsibility to others does not arise from their capacity for reason or language, but from their capacity to suffer, their vulnerability to violence, and their shared mortality. This vulnerability is not unique to humans; it is shared by all living beings. A posthumanist ethics de-centres human agency, focusing instead on our dependence on non-human systems and our shared exposure to ecological precarity:

This ethical project demands a transformation of our legal and political institutions, dismantling the speciesist laws that reduce non-human animals to property and developing new forms of trans-species justice. By recognising our shared vulnerability on a finite planet, critical posthumanism offers a framework for building a more sustainable and just world, where the power to dominate nature is replaced by a collective responsibility to care for the biosphere.
> "vibrant, rigorous posthumanism is vital for addressing questions of ethics and justice, language and trans-species communication, social systems and their inclusions and exclusions" (p. xvii)

chapters.title: 99. Lauren Berlant: Cruel Optimism

content.value: Lauren Berlant (1957–2021)
Original title: *Cruel Optimism*
2011 · English · United States · Affect Theory / Queer Theory / Cultural Studies · Theoretical Essays / Cultural Critique
## The Architecture of Compromised Desire: Defining Cruel Optimism

Lauren Berlant’s *Cruel Optimism*, published by Duke University Press in 2011, is a seminal work in contemporary affect theory, queer studies, and cultural criticism. Berlant’s central theoretical intervention is to conceptualise "cruel optimism", a specific affective structure that characterises the relation of desire under late neoliberalism. Optimism, in Berlant's formulation, is not a simple psychological mood or a positive attitude. Rather, optimism is the basic force that draws us out of ourselves and connects us to the world, project, or scene. Cruel optimism arises when this optimistic attachment becomes a direct threat to our survival or well-being:

Crucial to this concept is that the threat does not lie in the object of desire itself, but in the structural impossibility of its realisation under current historical conditions. Under late capitalism, the objects of our attachment, such as upward mobility, secure employment, home ownership, family stability, and democratic equality, are increasingly compromised. The economic and social safety nets that once subsidised the fantasy of the "good life" have been systematically dismantled. Yet, because these fantasies form the very horizon of what makes life meaningful and legible, the subject cannot simply choose to let them go. To abandon the attachment would mean to confront a state of absolute loss, disorientation, and subjective collapse. We remain bound to the very conditions that wear us out, maintaining a desperate attachment to a problematic object in advance of its loss.

> "A relation of cruel optimism exists when something you desire is actually an obstacle to your flourishing... \[These relations\] become cruel only when the object that draws your attachment actively impedes the aim that brought you to it initially" (p. 1)
## The Historical Present as an Impasse: Navigating Neoliberal Precarity

In the opening chapter of the monograph, Berlant examines how the historical present is experienced by the contemporary subject. Rather than a linear progression toward a better future, the present is experienced as an impasse. Drawing on Gilles Deleuze’s concept of the "any-space-whatever," Berlant defines the impasse as a temporal and spatial zone where the old genres of life no longer work, but new ones have not yet emerged. The post-Fordist transition to precarity has shattered the mid-century compromise of stable labour and social mobility, leaving the working and middle classes to navigate a state of permanent instability.

The impasse is not a temporary crisis that can be easily resolved; it is a chronic state of waiting, adjusting, and trying to find one’s footing in a shifting landscape. Berlant argues that our collective habits of thought are out of sync with our material reality. We continue to use the narrative genres of the mid-century welfare state to organise our desires, even though those genres are structurally obsolete. The experience of the present is therefore characterised by a kind of affective suspension, where we are caught in the act of trying to manage the gap between what we want and what is actually available. The impasse is the site where we feel the weight of history as a slow attrition, forcing us to develop new ways of coping with the loss of the stable futures we were promised.
## Slow Death and the Wear of the Body: The Biopolitics of Precarity

The third chapter of the monograph introduces the concept of slow death, which Berlant defines as the systematic physical wearing out of populations under late capitalism. Unlike the spectacular, sudden violence of war or state executions (such as those analysed in necropolitics), slow death is bureaucratic, routine, and almost invisible. It is the gradual, everyday attrition of biological life that occurs when the structural conditions of survival are compromised. Berlant focuses on the epidemic of obesity and related public health crises in marginalised communities as a primary manifestation of this slow death.

Under neoliberalism, the food and health industries operate to maximise profit, leaving the working class with access only to cheap, processed foods that cause long-term physical harm. At the same time, the privatisation of healthcare and the intensifications of the labour market leave individuals with little time or resources to care for their bodies. Slow death is not a temporary crisis, but a chronic condition that is normalised as a feature of daily life. The population is not subjected to sudden violence, but is rather allowed to wear out slowly through the gradual erosion of the material conditions of health and safety. In this context, obesity is not an individual pathology, but a physical registration of class inequality. The body becomes the primary site where the structural violence of the market is written, transforming the basic activities of nourishment into a slow destruction of the biological substrate. This slow death is a crucial tool of neoliberal biopolitics, which manages the population by allowing the most vulnerable to slowly wear out while maintaining the illusion of individual choice and responsibility. Crucially, Berlant challenges the moral pathologisation of obesity, which treats weight gain as an individual failure of willpower or reason. Instead, eating is understood as a form of lateral agency, a coping mechanism that offers immediate comfort and temporary relief from the exhausting precarity of daily life.
## Genre-Flailing and Lateral Agency: Surviving the Attrition of the Good Life

When the traditional genres of the good life collapse, the subject is forced into a state that Berlant calls genre-flailing. Genre-flailing describes the erratic, desperate attempts to find new ways of narrating and organising our lives when our old scripts no longer make sense. It is the feeling of trying out different lifestyles, political stances, or personal habits in a frantic attempt to find a secure place in the world. Genre-flailing is a symptom of our collective disorientation under late capitalism, registering the difficulty of building a stable identity when the material foundations of that identity have been pulled away.

In this state of disorientation, traditional models of political agency are often ineffective. Humanism has historically prioritised active, heroic agency aimed at structural transformation. Berlant argues that under the chronic precarity of the impasse, subjects often rely on lateral agency instead. Lateral agency is not about making a sovereign decision to change the world; it is about getting through the day, finding moments of respite, and maintaining one’s sanity. Drifting, eating, cruising, and zoning out are all forms of lateral agency that prioritise survival over transformation. While suspicious critics might dismiss these activities as politically regressive or passive, Berlant defends them as necessary coping mechanisms. In a world characterised by the slow attrition of the good life, lateral agency is the primary way we keep ourselves alive, preserving the capacity to feel and relate when the system demands our exhaustion.
## Towards a Common Life: The Postcritical Politics of Public Feelings

The ultimate ambition of Lauren Berlant’s *Cruel Optimism* is to sketch the outlines of a new politics of public feelings that can move beyond the limits of suspicious critique. Ideology critique is often stuck in a suspicious register, exposing the false promises of the American Dream or the lies of the state. While this critique is analytically correct, it often fails to connect with the affective attachments of the population. People do not hold onto the fantasy of the good life because they are stupid or deceived; they hold onto it because they need those attachments to survive.

A postcritical politics of public feelings seeks to address these attachments directly. It asks: how can we build new, less cruel forms of optimism? How can we create public spaces and common lives that do not demand the wear of our bodies and the exploitation of our labour? This postcritical approach requires a willingness to suspect our own habits of suspicion. Instead of merely exposing the lies of neoliberal ideology, critics must learn to listen to the desires and attachments of the population, recognising that these attachments represent a real, historical search for security and connection. By validating the emotional warmth of optimism while critiquing its cruel structures, postcritique opens up new possibilities for collective organising. It encourages us to build new networks of care and solidarity that can sustain us in the present, transforming the impasse from a zone of paralysis into a space of collective experimentation and shared survival. Berlant calls for the cultivation of a shared vulnerability, a collective recognition of our precarity on a finite planet, replacing the individualised pursuit of the good life with a collective commitment to sustaining one another.

chapters.title: 100. Rita Felski: The Limits of Critique

content.value: Rita Felski (1956–)
Original title: *The Limits of Critique*
2015 · English · United Kingdom / United States · Postcritique / Affect Theory / Actor-Network Theory · Theoretical Monograph / Literary Criticism Manifesto
## The Architecture of Suspicion: Critique as Mood and Method

Rita Felski’s *The Limits of Critique*, published by the University of Chicago Press in 2015, represents the definitive manifesto of the "postcritique" movement in contemporary literary studies. Felski’s central critical intervention is to subject the practice of critique itself to close rhetorical and sociological scrutiny. In the modern humanities, critique is more than one method among others; it is the de facto posture of literary interpretation, an institutionalised habit of mind that is treated as synonymous with intellectual rigour and political commitment. Felski argues that critique has become so ubiquitous that we have forgotten how to imagine alternative forms of rigorous thought:

To deconstruct this dominance, Felski analyses critique not as an objective, transparent science, but as a specific genre characterised by its own conventions, rhetoric, and mood. The mood of critique is typically aloof, suspicious, and highly vigilant. The critic stands in a position of intellectual superiority, reading against the grain to expose the text’s hidden political failures and ideological complicities. Felski argues that this suspicious mood restricts our engagement with literature, reducing the rich phenomenology of reading to a single, repetitive exercise in exposure. By treating the text as a patient to be diagnosed, critique overlooks the diverse ways literature actively informs, comforts, and transforms its readers.
> "suspicion is the de facto posture of literary interpretation... so habitual that we have forgotten how to imagine alternative forms of rigorous thought." (p. 3)
## The Critic as Detective: The Storytelling of Ferreting Things Out

A key rhetorical device analysed by Felski is the depiction of the critic as a detective. In symptomatic reading, the text is treated as a crime scene or a deceptive surface that hides a secret truth. The critic-as-detective uses their analytical skill to decode clues, connect disparate details, and expose the underlying ideological system that the text attempts to conceal. Felski argues that this ferreting out of hidden secrets is not an objective reporting of textual facts, but is itself a form of narrative construction:

This detective-like ferreting is particularly prominent in Marxist and psychoanalytic interpretations, where the text is assumed to be actively working to conceal its own trauma or complicity. The critic, like Sherlock Holmes, reads the minor symptoms, slips of the tongue, and structural gaps as clues to a hidden crime. But Felski points out that this narrative structure is highly selective: the critic must construct a neat, causal story that links the clues to a single, pre-determined culprit (such as the contradictions of capital or the repressed Oedipal desire). By forcing the text into this narrative template, the critic ignores the ways the text may be wrestling with multiple, conflicting questions, reducing its polyphony to a single, monolithic secret. By structuring their criticism as a detective story, critics create a highly satisfying narrative of demystification. The critic appears as a heroic investigator who rescues the text from its own ignorance, while the reader of the criticism is invited to share in this feeling of intellectual mastery. However, Felski warns that this detective model relies on a highly adversarial relationship with the text. It assumes that the work is always hiding something, that it is a deceptive structure designed to mislead the reader. This default suspicion blinds the critic to the text’s active disclosures, treating its explicit meanings as mere cover-ups rather than genuine insights into the social world.

> "Both detectives and critical readers, to quote Bloch once more, make it their goal to 'ferret things out.' Ferreting, I've been suggesting, is a matter of storytelling, of creating a compelling narrative." (p. 127)
## Spatial Metaphors of Critique: Digging Down and Standing Above

Felski examines two primary spatial metaphors that structure the practice of critique: digging down and standing above. The metaphor of digging down is central to symptomatic and deconstructive reading. It assumes that the true meaning of a text is not on its surface, but is buried deep within its structure. The critic’s task is to dig beneath the surface of the text to uncover the hidden political secrets, such as class conflict, racial exclusion, or gendered anxiety, that lie at the base of the work. This digging metaphor establishes a hierarchy where the surface of the text is treated as superficial, deceptive, or naive, while the depths are valued as the site of truth and critical insight.

The metaphor of standing above is characteristic of historicist and ideological criticism. Here, the critic places themselves in a position of historical or theoretical superiority, looking down on the text from a vantage point of advanced knowledge. The critic assumes that the text is blinded by its historical context, and that only the modern critic, equipped with Marxist, feminist, or postcolonial theory, can see the structural forces that shape the work. Felski critiques this spatial arrangement, showing that it places the critic in a position of invulnerability. By standing above the text, the critic is never forced to listen to it, to be challenged by it, or to acknowledge their own emotional attachment to it. Felski's critique of these spatial arrangements is not an argument for a flat, uncritical reading, but rather a call for a more relational geometry of interpretation. When we stand beside the text rather than above it, we allow ourselves to be influenced by its formal qualities and intellectual arguments. The text ceases to be a active object of our theoretical gaze and becomes an active partner in a shared inquiry. This shift in spatial orientation opens up new possibilities for critical reflection, allowing the reader to experience the text as a source of surprise, challenge, and transformation rather than a mere confirmation of what they already know. Postcritique seeks to dismantle these spatial hierarchies, encouraging a critical practice that stands alongside the text, treating it as an active co-producer of meaning.
## Actor-Network Theory and the Text: Postcritical Reading as Mediation

To construct a positive alternative to suspicious reading, Felski imports Bruno Latour’s actor-network theory into literary studies. In traditional critique, the text is treated as a passive effect of social causes, a mirror that reflects the interests of class, gender, or race. Latour’s sociology of association, by contrast, suggests that the social is not a hidden cause that explains the text; rather, the social is assembled through the interactions of diverse actors, both human and non-human. Felski argues that the literary work is an active mediator, a non-human actor that has the capacity to establish new connections, generate affects, and transform its environment.

Postcritical reading does not seek to look behind the text to find its social causes, nor does it stand above it to expose its historical limits. Instead, it traces the associations and attachments that the text builds. A text is not a self-contained container of meaning, but a node in a network: it connects with readers, other texts, institutions, historical memories, and physical spaces. Postcritical reading investigates how these connections are established and maintained. It asks: what does this text make possible? How does it move us? How does it associate with other actors to build a shared world? By treating the text as an active partner in a network, postcritical reading shifts the focus from exposure to association, re-establishing literature as an active participant in social life.
## Beyond the Hermeneutics of Suspicion: Reclaiming Attachment and Love

The ultimate ambition of Rita Felski’s *The Limits of Critique* is to liberate literary studies from the false choice between a suspicious, professionalised critique and a naive, uncritical appreciation. Felski calls for a critical practice that is honest about its own attachments, recognising that our love for literature is not a barrier to rigorous thought, but its very condition:

Postcritique does not mean a return to a naive, pre-theoretical impressionism, nor does it advocate for the abandonment of political vigilance. Rather, it calls for the expansion of our critical repertoire, encouraging scholars to develop new methods of reading that can accommodate attachment, enchantment, and translation. Felski’s work is a vital defence of the humanities, showing that the value of literary studies lies both in our capacity to expose the limits of our worlds and in our capacity to build new connections, to listen to the voices of the texts we read, and to reclaim reading as a collaborative project of shared survival and love.

> "What if we refused to be railroaded into the false choice between the critical and the uncritical? How might argument and interpretation proceed if critique were no longer our ubiquitous watchword and ever-vigilant watchdog? What other shapes of thought could we imagine? And how else might we venture to read, if we were not ordained to read suspiciously?" (p. 154)
